title: Incudo game system definition
description: The contract behind ADR 0011's promise: if a system definition validates against this schema, the app can build characters in it. This file is a public API — see ADR 0011 for the versioning policy. Validation here is STRUCTURAL, not semantic: a system can be valid and still be a poor model of its game, which is the author's business. What validating guarantees is that the app will not crash and will not silently misread the file.

formatVersion.description: The version of this format, not of the system. Bumped only by a breaking change to the format itself.

id.patternDescription: must be lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, e.g. "dnd5e" or "my-house-rules"

description.description: What this system is, in a sentence a player would read. The launcher shows it on a card, so it is user-facing prose — what the game is, who publishes it, what it feels like — and not a note to whoever maintains the definition. Notes for maintainers belong in systems/README.md.

version.description: The system definition's own version. Overlays record the parent version they were written against.

extends.description: The id of an official system this one overlays. ADR 0011.

elementTypes.description: The type vocabulary content may use — the list Aurora hardcodes.

stats.description: Stats shared by every character kind. A kind may add its own, or replace one by name.

generationMethods.description: How a build step's budget can produce its starting values (ADR 0017). Declared once for the system and referenced by id from a step's budget, because a PC and an NPC generate ability scores the same way and the cost table should not be written twice.

characterKinds.description: At least one. A system with no kinds can build nothing. ADR 0009.

auroraTypeMap.description: Aurora element types that map onto this system's types. Only needed to consume Aurora content.

logo.description: An image shown beside this system's name, as a reference and never inline bytes: an https: URL, or a path relative to this definition. ADR 0007 — Incudo's formats are JSON and images are never inlined. Optional; a system without one gets a card with no image, and the app draws no substitute (it generates no artwork, not even a placeholder).

suggestedSources.description: Content indexes to offer when the user adds a source (ADR 0031). Pointers, not content: a system definition still ships no elements (ADR 0022) and a character still opens with none configured (ADR 0012). They live on the system rather than in a catalogue beside the app so that a user-authored system can point at its own content, and a fork inherits what it was forked from. Nothing is fetched until the user picks one.

suggestedSource.description: One content index a system's author suggests. Adding it configures a source whose id is this url, verbatim.

official.description: The system definition's author vouches for this index. A CLAIM, NOT A CHECK — anyone can write true here in their own system, so a view must say who is vouching rather than presenting it as a verdict. It says nothing about the content's licence, quality or affiliation; the projects these point at belong to other people (ADR 0010).

licence.description: ADR 0010. Required on official systems; the app does not enforce it on user systems.

bound.description: A stat bound: a plain number, or an expression over stats. Applied to every stat — contributed, derived or both — after contributions and derivations settle and before overrides, which still win (ADR 0016). An expression is what the interesting bounds need: 5e's ability score maximum is `20 + strength:max`, because the corpus keeps only the delta and Aurora hardcodes the 20. Bounds read the unclamped values of other stats, in one pass.

expr.description: A stat expression. Deliberately not a scripting language: no loops, no I/O, and a fixed function set. Content comes from the internet.

oneOf.description: A number read out of a declared row, indexed by another expression (ADR 0018). For the published numbers that are a table and have no closed form: 5e's multiclass spell slots are twenty rows of nine. The index is floored and clamped to the array, so a value below the row reads its first entry and one above reads its last.

The sum of the character's recorded results matching a pattern, one per point of progression (ADR 0019). "hp:level:{n}" at level 8 sums hp:level:1 through hp:level:8. Reading only: the engine does not roll and must never learn how — a roll is an input precisely because it has no formula (ADR 0007). Bounded by the progression rather than by the record, so dropping a level stops counting the rolls above it without deleting them.

A setter read off the root element of the track being evaluated, as a number (ADR 0044). "dieSides" takes the face count of a dN value (d8 is 8) and is the one parsing rule; any other value reads 0. Only meaningful inside a trackStats value, which is the one place a track is known; anywhere else it reads 0 and the derivation reports a warning. The setter is named by the system (5e's hd), so the engine names no game noun.

progression.description: How a kind of character advances. ADR 0009.

stat.description: The stat the level is published as. Defaults to "level", which is what levelled content references.

elementIdPattern.description: An element id granted once per step of progression, with "{n}" replaced by the step number: "ID_LEVEL_{n}" gives a level 8 character ID_LEVEL_1 through ID_LEVEL_8. Aurora writes exactly those into every save and its content references them; without this, a character built in Incudo cannot match one built in Aurora. Only whole-numbered steps are granted.

trackStatPattern.description: The stat each track publishes its own count as, with "{name}" replaced by the track element name, lowercased: "level:{name}" on a character whose levels went to the Warlock element gives level:warlock = 18. A track is an element the character spent progression on (ADR 0015); grants inherit their granter’s track, so a class feature's level gate reads its own class's level rather than the character's total. 150-odd references in the Aurora corpus read these stats and nothing in the corpus writes them — Aurora computes them in application code. Omit it and no track stats are published.

trackType.description: The element type a track is rooted on (5e: "Class"). A character that has spent every point on one element records no advancement (ADR 0036), so it has no track to publish a count from; naming the type lets the engine treat the single element of that type it holds as an implicit track, which publishes its count and takes part in track stats and gates nothing (ADR 0044). Omit it and a single-track character publishes no track stats.

elementIdPattern.description: An element id granted once per step of progression, with "{n}" replaced by the step number: "ID_LEVEL_{n}" gives a level 8 character ID_LEVEL_1 through ID_LEVEL_8. Aurora writes exactly those into every save and its content references them; without this, a character built in Incudo cannot match one built in Aurora. Only whole-numbered steps are granted.

Omit it and no track stats are published.

characterKind.description: Only `id` is required, because a kind may `extends` another and state just its differences. A kind that extends nothing needs progression, elementTypes, buildSteps and sheet to be buildable — the app reports a kind missing those as unusable rather than refusing to load the system.

id.patternDescription: must be lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, e.g. "pc" or "legendary"

extends.description: The id of another kind in this system. "legendary" is a delta on "npc", not a copy of it.

elementTypes.description: When the kind extends another, an entry may be written "+Type" to add or "-Type" to remove; a list with no prefixed entry replaces the parent's outright.

grants.description: Element ids every character of this kind has without choosing them. The system-definition home for what Aurora answers in application code: a 5e character has a base armour class and adds its Constitution modifier to hit points, and no content file says so. Not stored on the character, so fixing the baseline fixes every character rather than only the ones saved afterwards.

repeatableSetter.description: The setter an element carries to say it may be taken more than once (ADR 0035). An element carrying it is offered again by a select that already holds it, and its rules apply once for every time the character chose it — a +1 to a score taken twice is +2. The name is the system's: Aurora spells it "allow duplicate". A kind that names none treats every element as taken at most once. Replaced rather than merged along an extends chain.

trackStat.description: A stat contributed once per track (ADR 0018). ADR 0015 gave every track a published count that content reads by name; this is the part that iterates — "for each track, add half its count" — which a system definition cannot write out, because content ships its own tracks. For every track the character has, if `when`'s element is in that track, `value` is evaluated and added to `stat`. Track contributions land with content's, before derivations read them.

stat.description: The stat contributed to. `{name}` is replaced with the track element's lowercased name, which turns an aggregate into a per-track stat: "{name}:spellcasting:solo" publishes warlock:spellcasting:solo. Without it, every track's contribution sums into one stat.

when.description: Only contribute for tracks containing this element. Omit to contribute for every track. This is the hook content already provides: a 5e casting class grants a marker saying which weighting it uses, and the marker lands in that class's track.

value.description: Evaluated once per matching track. The reserved reference "track:progress" reads that track's own count.

blockStat.description: A stat contributed once per declared block (ADR 0020). An element may declare named blocks — Aurora's <spellcasting name="Bard" ability="Charisma"> is the corpus's only kind — and content keys stats on those names. It is a third keying, not a second: the block's name is not the track's, so an Eldritch Knight's stats live under "eldritch knight" while its track is "fighter", and trackStats' {name} substitutes the wrong word. For every distinct block name the character's elements declare, `value` is evaluated and added to `stat`. Block contributions land with content's and with trackStats', before derivations read them.

stat.description: The stat contributed to. `{name}` is the block's lowercased name, so "{name}:spellcasting:dc" publishes bard:spellcasting:dc — which is the key content already contributes item bonuses to. Any other `{key}` reads that attribute off the block.

value.description: Evaluated once per block. Placeholders resolve inside a `ref`'s stat name too, so "{ability}:modifier" reads charisma:modifier for the Bard and intelligence:modifier for the Wizard. An entry with a placeholder the block does not declare contributes nothing and is reported.

blockFilter.description: How a $(key) in a select's filter expands, for a rule attached to a declared block (ADR 0030). The fourth thing a declared block does, after ADR 0020's three keyings of a stat, and the same framing: a rule may be attached to a named block, and its filter is written in terms of what that block and the derivation publish. The keys cannot live in the engine — Aurora's two both spell a word the engine is not allowed to know — so they are declared here, beside the rest of the system's vocabulary. Declare either `tags` or `tagsFromStats`; when both are given, `tags` is tried first. An expansion that legitimately finds nothing matches nothing and is not reported as unresolved, so "you have no spell slots yet" and "Incudo cannot read this filter" stay different sentences.

key.description: The interpolation key as content writes it, without the $( and the ). Compared lowercased.

tags.description: Ordered alternatives over the block's name and attributes, written with the same {name} and {attribute} placeholders blockStats uses. The FIRST entry whose placeholders all resolve wins — a fallback chain, not an OR, because the alternatives disagree on purpose: an Eldritch Knight's block is named "Eldritch Knight" and its list is "Wizard,(Abjuration||Evocation)", and OR-ing them would offer the whole wizard list. Whatever the winning entry expands to is parsed as a supports sub-expression, so it may be a group rather than one tag.

tagsFromStats.description: Stat-name patterns, each carrying exactly one *, which matches a single :-delimited segment. Every stat the derivation settled that matches a pattern and holds a POSITIVE value contributes its captured segment as a tag, and the whole is an OR. This is how "any level you have slots for" is written without the engine learning what a slot is; it widens on its own as the character levels, because the stats it reads are the ones content and the system already publish. Placeholders resolve first, so "{name}:spellcasting:slots:*" reads the block's own table and "spellcasting:slots:*" the shared one.

fillFrom.description: Emit every integer from here up to the largest numeric capture, instead of the captures themselves; non-numeric captures are still emitted verbatim. The system's way of saying "a resource published at one level covers everything at or below it". 5e needs it because a warlock's pact table publishes exactly one positive slot level — 5th at high level — while the character really can pick spells of every level up to it.

candidateNote.description: A short fact a picker prints beside a candidate of certain types — a spell's level, say. Which setter says it and how it reads are the system's business, because the engine does not know that a spell has a level or that level 0 is called a cantrip. The text becomes part of the candidate's label, so a search matches it too: typing "cantrip" narrows a spell list to cantrips. A candidate without the setter gets no note. Replaced rather than merged along an extends chain; a kind that declares none prints a name and a source.

types.description: Element types the note is printed for.

setter.description: The setter whose value is shown.

label.description: The text, with {value} standing for the setter's value.

contribution.description: A stat this kind contributes itself, optionally only when a condition holds (ADR 0022). The base case trackStats and blockStats are iterating specialisations of: those contribute once per track and once per declared block, and this contributes once, for a character of this kind. What it adds is a `requirements`, which is what a conditional baseline rule needs and neither of the others can give it — "a character wearing no armour has an armour class of 10" is a statement about the character, not about any element it holds. Contributions land with content's own stat rules and in the same bonus buckets, before derivations read them. They belong here and not on an element the kind grants: a kind's grants are copied into every save, and a rule copied into a save is frozen at the moment the file was written, while system.json is the one thing a save deliberately does not embed.

bonus.description: Named bonus bucket, exactly as on a content <stat>. Two contributions sharing a bucket do not stack — the largest wins — which is how a feat's larger number replaces a system's without knowing what the system wrote.

requirements.description: A condition in content's own requirement language, as a string: "[armor:medium]", "![armor:heavy]". Not a JSON tree, because a system definition is authored by hand and its author has already read this spelling a thousand times in content. Named `requirements` and not `when` so a reader who knows content knows it instantly — trackStats' `when` is an element id and means something else. An expression that will not parse makes the system invalid.

inventory.description: How this kind reads the setters content puts on an item (ADR 0025). The mechanism behind `equipped="[armor:none]"`, which the Aurora corpus carries on 78 rules. A slot publishes a *set of tags* rather than one string, because the twelve operands the corpus uses are three different kinds of thing: `heavy` is the value of a setter, `versatile` is the *presence* of one (the setter's value is a die), and `double-bladed scimitar` is the element's own name. A kind with no inventory evaluates no `equipped=` condition and gates nothing on attunement — the same way a kind with no progression ignores `level=` instead of reading every gate as unmet.

slotSetter.description: The setter naming where an item goes. 5e's content writes `slot`, on 1,070 elements. A bag entry's own `slot` overrides it, and means the user put the item somewhere the element did not say.

occupiedTag.description: What an occupied slot publishes whatever is in it. The corpus asks for this as `any`.

emptyTag.description: What a declared slot with nothing in it publishes, and nothing else. The corpus asks for this as `none`, 56 times.

tagSetters.description: Setters whose *value* becomes a tag, lowercased: 5e's `armor` setter turns a Plate into `heavy`. Taken verbatim — on 102 corpus elements that setter means something else entirely, and that is harmless only because adorners occupy no slot.

flagSetters.description: Setters whose *presence* becomes a tag, named after the setter rather than its value. `<set name="versatile">1d8</set>` is how a quarterstaff says it is versatile, and `[primary:versatile]` is the corpus asking; the die is not what the question is about.

slot.description: One place a character may put an item. `id` is compared verbatim against the slot setter's value, so it is content's word and not the system's: 5e's two shields say `onehand,secondary` and that whole string is the shield slot's id.

stats.description: The stats this slot publishes into, in fill order — and therefore its capacity, since one stat holds one item. `["armor"]` is one suit of armour; `["primary", "secondary"]` is two hands and an item takes the first that is free. Omit for a slot that publishes nothing, which then holds any number of things: 5e has no rule about how many cloaks you may wear, and declaring one here would be inventing it.

attunement.description: How this system marks an item as requiring attunement (ADR 0023). An equipped item that requires it and is not attuned contributes none of its rules, and a warning names it. Its setters are untouched, so it still weighs what it weighs; and because a magic adorner is a separate element from its mundane host, gating one leaves an unattuned Flame Tongue greatsword a working greatsword.

requires.description: The setter value meaning "this requires attunement". Not decoration: 5e's corpus writes `true` on 968 elements and `false` on 8.

countStat.description: The stat the count of attuned items is contributed to (ADR 0023 decision 3). One attuned *entry* is one attunement, because a magic item is modelled as a mundane host plus a magical adorner and the flag sits on the instance. A contribution rather than a published input, so that content contributing to the same key is not discarded.

maxStat.description: The stat holding the limit. A character over it is reported, never refused. The base belongs in the kind's `contributions` and not in a StatDef `default` — a default is a base that contributions add to, so a default of 3 plus a feature's bonus="base" 4 would read 7 instead of 4.

types.description: May be empty: a step can be about entering numbers rather than picking elements.

multiple.description: This step is answered by a set: zero or more of its candidates, never blocking (ADR 0032). For a system's optional rules, where choosing none is the ordinary answer. Cannot be combined with `required`. A reader that does not know this key builds the character without the set, so it does not change formatVersion.

requires.description: Ids of steps that must be usable before this one is (ADR 0017). A genuine dependency and nothing else — you cannot pick spells before something makes you a spellcaster. The suggested order is a topological sort of these with the declared array order breaking ties, so a step that requires nothing sorts first; a step whose dependencies are unmet is not yet available rather than skippable.

priority.description: Where this step's own pick, and everything answering it opens, ranks among "Open decisions" — lower sorts first. Defaults to this step's position in the declared/topological build order, so a system that never sets it keeps that order unchanged. Independent of `requires`, which decides when a step can be reached rather than where it reads once it can be — a system author who wants an unanswered Background to keep outranking an already-open Class select states that here, by giving `background` a lower number than `class`, rather than the app enforcing one universal reading for every system.

levelRoll.description: A per-level recorded roll a perLevel step owns (ADR 0019) — 5e's hit points, and anything shaped like them. The engine already sums character.rolls through a `rolls` expression; what varies per character, and what content already declares, is which die a given level owes. `classType` names the element type that governs a level (5e's "Class"); when the character's advancement does not record which element that was for a given level — every character built in the app today, with no multiclass UI yet — the character's single element of that type stands in for all of them, the same fallback the engine itself uses for an element in no track.

pattern.description: The key a roll is recorded under, with {n} replaced by the level — "hp:level:{n}". Matches the pattern the stat's own `rolls` derive reads.

dieSetter.description: The setter naming the die, read off the governing element. Aurora's content writes this as `hd`, e.g. `<set name="hd">d6</set>`.

classType.description: The element type whose single instance on the character governs a level's die, absent a recorded advancement entry for that level.

fixedWhen.description: An element id (5e's use-average-hit-points campaign option, ADR 0044). While the character has it every level's value is fixed at the die's average instead of rolled: the builder publishes it and opens no decision, and rolls already recorded stay recorded and unread.

budget.description: A pool of points a build step distributes (ADR 0017). `stat` is an ordinary stat, so content adds to it with the `stat` rule that already exists — a feat, a race variant, an improvement at level 4 — and the step reopens on its own when it does. That is the answer to "a class gave you one more attribute point and you should not have to walk back to an earlier screen".

methods.description: Ids of the system's generationMethods this step offers.

generationMethod.description: How a budget's starting values are produced (ADR 0017). Data rather than code, because docs/CODE-REUSE-POLICY.md rule 1 says a rule about the game may not live in a component, and a point-buy cost table is exactly that. Three shapes: `pool` plus `costs` is a points method; `values`, or `dice` with `count`, hands out a set to assign; neither means the user types numbers.

dice.description: Dice notation the shell rolls, e.g. "4d6dl1". Core never rolls anything.

perBlock.description: Render this section once per block the character declares, substituting the block's name and attributes into every entry of `stats` (ADR 0020). Needed because blockStats publishes keys a section cannot name: there is no bard:spellcasting:dc in any system definition and there never can be, because the key comes from content. The flag is also what makes `{name}` mean something here — elsewhere it names the subject of an iteration, and a sheet section iterates nothing until it says what it iterates.
